title: What is good retention? Benchmarks for user and net revenue retention by business type
summary: Lenny and Casey Winters polled 20 growth experts to set GOOD and GREAT benchmarks for 6-month user retention and 12-month net revenue retention across consumer, SMB and enterprise models. It also explains when lower retention is acceptable and why retention is the most telling metric for a business.

principles.text: Retention is the scalable way to grow and the best signal of product-market fit; no metric predicts thrive-or-die better.
principles.quote: No other metric is as singularly telling of whether your business will thrive or die.

principles.text: Benchmark user retention by business type: consumer social ~25% good/45% great; enterprise SaaS ~70% good/90% great at 6 months.
principles.quote: Consumer social: ~25% is GOOD, ~45% is GREAT

principles.text: Benchmark net revenue retention: bottom-up SaaS ~100% good, ~120% great; enterprise ~110% good, ~130% great.
principles.quote: Bottom-up SaaS: ~100% is GOOD, ~120% is GREAT

principles.text: Low retention can be OK if CAC and marginal costs are low, since cheap acquisition lets you afford to lose users.
principles.quote: If you can acquire new users cheaply (e.g. SEO, word of mouth, or virality), you can afford to lose more users.

principles.text: Growth is a balance of CAC, retention and unit economics; retention doesn't live in a vacuum.
principles.quote: Growth is a balancing act between CAC, retention, and unit economics.

principles.text: Not every business needs venture-scale retention; a flat retention curve enabling scalable acquisition can sustain a business.
principles.quote: a flat retention curve that drives a scalable acquisition strategy is enough to keep your business alive.
